title: "Euler 125"
format: html
date: '2026-08-25'

---


Finding the sum of palindromic numbers under a given limit, that can be expressed as the sum of consecutive squares.


Generating all possible numbers that can be expressed as a sum of consecutive 
squares is surprisingly quick.

For a given number we have to add two consecutive square numbers. The largest of
them can not be larger than half of that number. And we need the square root of
that number because we are adding square numbers.

That give us an upper limit. We then square a vector containing all numbers from
1 to that limit.

We need to add consecutive numbers in that squared vector. We need sums from position 1 to position 2, 3, 4, 5 etc. And from position 2 to positions 3, 4, 5, 6 etc.

Getting all the sums from position 1 to any given other position in the squared 
vector can be done by using the `cumsum` function. 

The challenge is to also, efficiently, get those beginning from position 2, 3 etc.

The `lead` function from `dplyr` can do that trick, we just need to provide it
with all the possible startpostions, and set `default = 0` to avoid having to handle `NA`s.

So, `lead` on `(0:limit)^2` with `n` set to all possible start positions. And the
the `cumsum`.

That give us a list of vectors. A lot of values will be repeated, we get rid of those.
And the first value in each vector will represent only one squared value, and we
need sums of squared values, so we also remove the first element in each vector. We can then unlist, remove duplicates and results that are too large. And get a vector - with just under 25 million values...

```{r eval = FALSE}
limit <- ceiling(sqrt(10^8/2))
possible_squares <- lapply(1:limit,
                           FUN = \(x) cumsum(dplyr::lead((0:limit)^2, 
                           n = x, 
                           default = 0)))  |> 
                    lapply(X = _, 
                           FUN = \(x) unique(x)) |> 
                    lapply(\(x) x[-1])  |> 
                    unlist() |> 
                    unique() |> 
                    (\(x) x[x < 10^8])()
```

That was surprisingly quick. Not quick, but not as slow as I expected.

We can now check which of these numbers are palindromic.

The simple way is to use the `stringi::stri_reverse` function:
```{r eval = FALSE}
hits <- possible_squares[possible_squares == stringi::stri_reverse(possible_squares)]
```

There are duplicates, and some of the values are too large:

```{r eval = FALSE}
answer <- sum(hits)
```

## An alternative


As an alternative we can generate palindromic numbers.

Those can be described as a first half followed by a second half that is the 
first half reversed. Separated by either nothing or a digit 0-9.

This method does not find the palindromic numbers 1-9, so we add them.

```{r eval = FALSE}

palindromes <- function(limit){
      n_digits <- ceiling(log10( limit))/2
      dig_limit <- as.numeric(paste(rep(9, n_digits), collapse = ""))
      digits_first <- 1:dig_limit |> as.character()
      digits_last <- stringi::stri_reverse(digits_first)
      center <- c(0:9, "")
      paste0(rep(digits_first, each = length(center)),
             rep(center,times = length(digits_first)),
             rep(digits_last, each = length(center))) |> 
      as.numeric() |> 
      (\(x) c(x, 1:9))()
}

possible_palindromes <- palindromes(10^8)

```

We can then locate the possible palindromes that are included in the 
vector containing the possible squares.

```{r eval = FALSE}
answer <- sum(possible_palindromes[possible_palindromes %in% possible_squares])
```
